title: AATS Expert Consensus: Surgical Management of Esophageal and GEJ Cancer
journal: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
breakthrough: The American Association for Thoracic Surgery convened an international, multidisciplinary panel — gastroenterologists, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, surgical oncologists and thoracic surgeons — to produce consensus recommendations on treating esophageal and gastroesophageal junction cancer at every stage, including the difficult scenarios. Developed by modified Delphi method with expert opinion where evidence was thin, it addresses the role of surgery, endoscopic therapy and surveillance in early-stage adenocarcinoma; how to combine surgery with multimodality therapy in locally advanced adenocarcinoma; and when to operate for squamous cell carcinoma.
impact: Esophagectomy's place has shifted underneath the specialty as endoscopic resection, systemic therapy and radiation have all improved. A consensus that treats each histology and stage separately, rather than issuing one pathway, matches how these decisions are actually made.
practical: The document's value is in the grey zones — margin requirements, extent of two-field lymphadenectomy, and what surveillance looks like after complete endoscopic mucosal resection when no esophagectomy has been done. Note the method: modified Delphi with expert opinion means these are consensus statements, not trial results, and where the panel could not agree the honest reading is that the question is open. Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma are handled as different diseases here, which is the right instinct and worth carrying into the tumour board.
link: The 2025 AATS expert consensus document: surgical management of esophageal and gastroesophageal junction cancer

verify.status: matched with corrections — document confirmed, recommendation count unverified
verify.note: Confirmed: 'The 2025 American Association for Thoracic Surgery (AATS) expert consensus document: Surgical management of esophageal and gastroesophageal junction cancer', JTCVS 2025, volume 170 issue 3, pages 884–901, international multidisciplinary panel, modified Delphi. The submission's description of the scope — early-stage, locally advanced adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, endoscopic resection versus radical esophagectomy, margins, two-field lymphadenectomy, post-EMR surveillance — matches the published abstract closely. Two adjustments: the '23 evidence-based recommendations' figure could not be verified in accessible sources and has been dropped rather than asserted; and the submission calls the recommendations 'evidence-based' without qualification, where the document itself states they rest on modified Delphi consensus and expert opinion — that distinction has been restored because it changes how much weight a reader should give a statement in a grey zone. Also removed the submission's claim that the document 'standardizes surgical pathways', which overstates a consensus statement.

title: CHEST Clinical Practice Guideline: Early-Stage Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
breakthrough: The American College of Chest Physicians issued a new clinical practice guideline for stage I and II NSCLC. For clinical stage I, it makes a STRONG recommendation for minimally invasive approaches over thoracotomy — on LOW certainty evidence, supported by the first meta-analysis to show an overall survival association favouring minimally invasive surgery. For clinical stage II, minimally invasive surgery is a CONDITIONAL recommendation. New evidence is cited showing equivalent overall survival for peripheral NSCLC of 2 cm or less treated by sublobar resection versus lobectomy. On systemic therapy: adjuvant chemotherapy plus a checkpoint inhibitor improves overall survival in resected stage II including node-negative tumours 4 cm or larger, and adjuvant targeted therapy improves overall survival in resected stage IB (3 cm or more) and stage II EGFR-mutant disease.
impact: It settles the open-versus-minimally-invasive question for stage I with the strongest recommendation the evidence will bear, and it folds the adjuvant immunotherapy and targeted-therapy results into a surgical guideline — which is where the surgeon's referral obligation now sits.
practical: Read the two recommendation strengths as different instructions: stage I is strong, stage II is conditional, and the certainty of evidence behind the stage I recommendation is LOW — so a thoracotomy in a difficult stage II case is not a guideline deviation. Systematic intraoperative mediastinal and hilar nodal sampling or dissection is required in both stages; without it the pathological stage is unreliable and the adjuvant decision is made on bad information. The sublobar equivalence applies to PERIPHERAL tumours 2 cm or less, which is the population the randomised trials studied — do not extend it upward on the strength of this guideline.
link: Management of patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer: an American College of Chest Physicians clinical practice guideline

verify.status: corrected — recommendation strength overstated, and the guideline's key surgical finding was omitted
verify.note: The guideline is real: CHEST, published July 2025 (PubMed 40562304). Corrections. (1) The submission says it 'formally establishes minimally invasive surgical resection (VATS or RATS) as the IMPERATIVE standard over open thoracotomy for clinical Stage I NSCLC'. The published recommendation is STRONG but on LOW CERTAINTY evidence for stage I, and for stage II it is only CONDITIONAL — the submission collapses two different strengths into one absolute. (2) The submission omits the guideline's most surgically consequential new statement: equivalent overall survival for peripheral ≤2 cm NSCLC treated by SUBLOBAR resection versus lobectomy. Restored, with the size limit stated, because the adjacent entry in this same list extends sublobar resection to 2–3 cm on weaker evidence. (3) 'Confirms routine adjuvant systemic therapy for resected Stage II disease' is imprecise — the guideline specifies chemotherapy PLUS checkpoint inhibitor, and separately adjuvant targeted therapy for EGFR-mutant stage IB(≥3 cm)/II. (4) The '17 evidence-based recommendations' count could not be verified and has been dropped. Added the systematic nodal sampling requirement, which the guideline states and the submission reduced to 'consistent post-resection pathological staging'.

title: NCCN Lung Cancer Screening v1.2025: No Limit on Years Since Quitting
journal: Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
breakthrough: NCCN removed the years-since-quitting restriction from its lung cancer screening criteria. Screening is now recommended for anyone aged 50 or older with a 20 pack-year or greater smoking history, with NO limit on how long ago they stopped. The rationale is that people who formerly smoked carry a substantially higher lung cancer risk than those who never smoked, and there is no substantive drop-off in that risk beyond 15 years since quitting — the cut-off the USPSTF adopted in 2021 and NCCN has now abandoned.
impact: It expands eligibility to a group that had been aging out of screening precisely as their incidence peaked. For thoracic surgery the consequence is downstream: more screen-detected stage I nodules in older former smokers, and therefore more candidates for anatomical sublobar resection.
practical: The practical friction is that NCCN and the USPSTF now disagree, and in the United States insurance coverage follows the USPSTF and CMS, not NCCN — so a patient 18 years past quitting may meet the NCCN criterion and still face a coverage problem. Check before promising a scan. Clinically, the expanded group is older and more comorbid, which raises the value of pulmonary function and cardiac assessment before a nodule becomes a resection discussion, and makes sublobar resection more often the right operation rather than a compromise.
link: NCCN Guidelines Insights: Lung Cancer Screening, Version 1.2025

verify.status: matched — verified, with the coverage mismatch added
verify.note: Fully verified. NCCN Guidelines Insights: Lung Cancer Screening, Version 1.2025 (JNCCN 23(1)): screening recommended at age ≥50 with ≥20 pack-years and NO limit on years since quitting; the stated rationale is that risk in people who formerly smoked remains substantially elevated with no substantive drop-off after 15 years since quitting. The submission's description is accurate, including the point that the 15-year restriction was the one removed and that the effect is to expand the pool of screen-detected stage I candidates. One addition of my own, not a correction: NCCN and USPSTF now differ on this criterion and US coverage tracks the USPSTF, so eligibility by NCCN does not guarantee a covered scan — a reader acting on this entry needs to know that before telling a patient they qualify.

title: Robotic Versus VATS Resection After Neoadjuvant Chemoimmunotherapy
journal: Journal of Thoracic Disease / Journal of Robotic Surgery (meta-analysis)
breakthrough: Comparative series and a meta-analysis address a problem neoadjuvant immunotherapy created: dense hilar and mediastinal fibrosis that makes a planned minimally invasive resection difficult. In a comparative cohort, conversion to thoracotomy occurred in 7.5% of robotic cases against 28.2% of VATS cases (P<0.001); the meta-analysis found robotic surgery associated with lower conversion (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.13–0.65; P=0.003), more lymph nodes dissected (MD 4.04) and more nodal stations explored (MD 1.22). Nodal assessment differed accordingly — yp-N0 in 88.5% versus 67.6%, yp-N2 in 3.8% versus 19.7%. Rates of complete resection, operative duration, blood loss and transfusion were not meaningfully different.
impact: The clinical question is whether a minimally invasive approach survives contact with a post-immunotherapy hilum, and on these data the robotic platform converts less often and samples more nodes. Both approaches showed equivalent perioperative and oncological safety.
practical: Interpret the nodal numbers carefully. More nodes and stations retrieved is a real advantage, but the accompanying yp-N0 versus yp-N2 difference reflects the populations being compared as much as the instrument — a retrospective series where more nodes are found in one arm and more N2 disease in the other is describing two different case mixes, not proving a staging superiority. The defensible statement is that robotic dissection maintains a minimally invasive approach through post-treatment fibrosis with more thorough nodal sampling. Have a plan for conversion regardless of platform: 7.5% is not zero, and a fibrotic hilum is the situation where an unplanned conversion goes badly.
link: Robotic-assisted versus video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery for NSCLC after neoadjuvant immunotherapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis

verify.status: corrected — the conversion figures are wrong, and no guideline update exists
verify.note: The clinical claim is supported but the numbers are not. The submission states conversion of '3.1% vs. 8.9%' for RATS versus VATS; the published comparative figures are 7.5% versus 28.2% (P<0.001), with a meta-analysis OR of 0.28 — both arms are substantially higher than submitted, and the gap is much wider. Corrected. The submission also claims the finding 'updates thoracic surgical society guidelines to recommend robotic platforms for complex post-immunotherapy hilar dissections and high-station N2 lymphadenectomy'; no such society guideline could be found, and that sentence has been removed. 'Multi-center trial analyses' overstates the evidence, which is retrospective comparative series plus a meta-analysis of them — restated. Retained and verified: lower conversion, higher node and station counts, no difference in complete resection/operative time/blood loss, and equivalent perioperative and oncological safety. Added a caution on the yp-N0/yp-N2 contrast, which the submission did not report and which is more likely case-mix than staging superiority.

title: Segmentectomy Versus Lobectomy in 2–3 cm (T1c) NSCLC
breakthrough: A national propensity-matched analysis compared anatomical segmentectomy with lobectomy in NSCLC of 2–3 cm — T1c, above the size range the randomised sublobar trials studied. No difference in overall survival was found between segmentectomy and lobectomy in either multivariable-adjusted or propensity score-matched analysis for clinical T1c disease; in the pathological T1cN0M0 subset, five-year survival was 74.1% versus 74.0%. The conclusion was that segmentectomy is non-inferior to lobectomy for clinical or pathological T1c NSCLC in a national dataset.
impact: JCOG0802 and CALGB140503 established sublobar resection for peripheral tumours of 2 cm or less. This extends the question upward, where no randomised answer exists, and finds no survival penalty in a matched observational comparison.
practical: This is propensity-matched registry data, not a randomised trial, and observational matching cannot remove the selection that determines who gets a segmentectomy for a 2.5 cm tumour in the first place. It is a reason to consider segmentectomy in a patient with limited pulmonary reserve where lobectomy is a real functional cost — not a reason to prefer it. Whatever the resection, the nodal dissection has to be complete: sublobar resection with inadequate nodal sampling is how an occult N1 goes unfound and adjuvant therapy is never offered. One claim to discard: matched analysis in patients WITH lymphovascular invasion showed no significant difference between segmentectomy and lobectomy either, so LVI is not the switch that makes lobectomy mandatory.
link: Segmentectomy vs lobectomy for patients with 2- to 3-cm non-small cell lung cancer

verify.status: REVERSED on the stratification claim — LVI does not make lobectomy mandatory
verify.note: The study is real (CHEST 2025, S0012-3692(25)00812-8) and its headline finding — segmentectomy non-inferior to lobectomy in T1c, five-year survival 74.1% vs 74.0% in pathological T1cN0M0 — is confirmed. The submission's clinical rule is not. It states that segmentectomy achieves equivalent recurrence-free survival 'in T1c tumors LACKING VPI/LVI, while lobectomy remains MANDATORY if microvascular/pleural invasion is present'. The published propensity-matched analysis found NO significant difference between segmentectomy and lobectomy in patients WITH lymphovascular invasion — the opposite of a mandate. No source supporting a VPI/LVI-conditional rule could be found, and it is the kind of invented decision rule that reads authoritative and changes an operation. Also corrected: 'propensity-matched trial data' — propensity matching is what you do in the ABSENCE of a trial, and calling it trial data hides the confounding that matters most here; and the submission omits that the randomised evidence for sublobar resection stops at 2 cm, which is the single most important caveat for a 2–3 cm tumour.

title: Postoperative ctDNA as a Prognostic Marker After NSCLC Resection
breakthrough: Meta-analyses of postoperative circulating tumour DNA in resected NSCLC establish it as a strong prognostic marker. In one synthesis of 13 studies and 1,309 patients, immediate postoperative ctDNA detection (4 studies, n=556) carried a hazard ratio of 6.41 (95% CI 4.18–9.83) for recurrence-free survival; a second, of 7 studies and 1,138 patients, found increased risk of both recurrence and death with ctDNA positivity. ctDNA positivity immediately after surgery or after adjuvant chemotherapy is more strongly associated with worse recurrence-free and overall survival than negativity, and clearance after radical therapy is associated with prolonged survival. Tumour-informed assays are the more specific; tumour-agnostic approaches are more sensitive in some settings.
impact: A hazard ratio above 6 for recurrence identifies a group that will relapse, months before imaging shows it. As a prognostic marker in resected NSCLC, ctDNA is now well evidenced.
practical: Prognostic is not the same as actionable, and this is where the field currently is. No randomised trial has shown that changing adjuvant treatment on the basis of a ctDNA result improves outcomes in NSCLC, and neither NCCN nor ASCO recommends ctDNA to guide adjuvant decisions or routine post-resection surveillance outside a trial. A positive result identifies risk without providing an intervention proven to modify it; a negative result does not license omitting adjuvant therapy that stage-based evidence supports. Enrol these patients in trials rather than escalating or de-escalating on the number — and know which assay type was used, because specificity and sensitivity differ between tumour-informed and tumour-agnostic platforms.
link: Prognostic value of postoperative circulating tumour DNA for recurrence-free survival in resected NSCLC: a systematic review and meta-analysis

verify.status: corrected — cohort size unverified, and guideline integration REVERSED
verify.note: The prognostic evidence is real and has been retained with actual figures (HR 6.41 for RFS on immediate postoperative detection; 13 studies/1,309 patients and 7 studies/1,138 patients). Three corrections. (1) The submission's '3,280+ resected NSCLC patients' could not be verified; the locatable meta-analyses are roughly a third of that, and the figure has been replaced with what is sourced. (2) The submission states this 'integrates post-resection ctDNA clearance as a high-confidence prognostic biomarker in NCCN and ASCO POST-SURGICAL SURVEILLANCE PROTOCOLS'. Neither society recommends ctDNA for routine post-resection surveillance in NSCLC; that sentence is removed and the actual position stated. (3) The submission says the result guides 'the escalation or de-escalation of adjuvant chemotherapy'. No randomised trial has shown ctDNA-guided adjuvant decisions improve NSCLC outcomes — and de-escalation on a negative ctDNA means withholding therapy with a proven stage-based survival benefit, which is the direction with real potential for harm. Restated explicitly. Retained from the submission and verified: lead time over radiological relapse, and the tumour-informed versus tumour-agnostic distinction.

title: Biomarker Selection for Perioperative Immunotherapy in Resectable NSCLC
breakthrough: The perioperative immunotherapy trials define their own boundaries by whom they enrolled. CheckMate 816 EXCLUDED patients with known EGFR or ALK alterations; KEYNOTE-671 permitted them but did not mandate testing. Both trials significantly improved event-free survival and pathological complete response with chemoimmunotherapy — KEYNOTE-671 in resectable stage II–IIIB with perioperative pembrolizumab. On PD-L1, higher expression was generally associated with greater benefit, but significant improvements were seen even in patients with low or negative PD-L1.
impact: The practical instruction is a testing one: molecular profiling has to happen BEFORE the perioperative treatment decision, not after resection, because an EGFR or ALK alteration changes the pathway and the pivotal trials provide no evidence for chemoimmunotherapy in that group.
practical: Be precise about why EGFR/ALK patients are steered elsewhere. It is not that a subgroup analysis showed immunotherapy fails them — it is that the trial that defined the standard EXCLUDED them, so there is no evidence either way from that programme, and separate experience of immune-related toxicity when checkpoint inhibitors and EGFR TKIs are given in sequence argues for caution. Absence of evidence is the honest reason, and it still supports the same decision. On PD-L1: do not use a low or negative result to withhold perioperative chemoimmunotherapy, because benefit was demonstrated in those patients too. Get tissue adequate for full molecular testing at diagnosis; a small biopsy that cannot be profiled is what forces this decision to be made blind.
link: Perioperative immunotherapy in resectable NSCLC — CheckMate 816 and KEYNOTE-671

verify.status: corrected — the reasoning is exclusion, not subgroup analysis, and the PD-L1 claim is overstated
verify.note: The clinical bottom line the submission reaches — profile for EGFR/ALK before committing to perioperative immunotherapy — is right, and both trials are real. Two corrections to how it gets there. (1) The submission says 'Phase III trial subgroup ANALYSES CONFIRMED that PD-L1 expression levels and targetable driver mutations (EGFR/ALK) dictate the efficacy of perioperative immune checkpoint blockade.' For EGFR/ALK there was no such subgroup analysis in the defining trial: CheckMate 816 EXCLUDED those patients, and KEYNOTE-671 allowed them without mandating testing. The recommendation rests on absence of evidence plus toxicity concerns, not on a demonstrated lack of benefit — a distinction that matters if a reader is ever asked to justify it. (2) 'maximizing pathological complete response in high-PD-L1 candidates' implies PD-L1 selects who should be treated; the trials showed significant benefit even at low or negative PD-L1, so a low value must not be used to withhold treatment. Restated. Removed the submission's unsourced claim about 'surgical delays' as a documented harm, and its assertion that guidelines now formally 'advise against' perioperative immunotherapy in this group, which could not be verified as written.

title: DECIPHER-NODL: Imaging Plus cfDNA Fragmentomics for Pulmonary Nodules
journal: The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific
breakthrough: DECIPHER-NODL is the first model to combine deep-learning low-dose CT radiomics with a cell-free DNA model built on four genome-wide fragmentation features — copy number variation, fragment size ratio, fragment-based methylation and motif signatures — through a stacked ensemble algorithm. The integrated imaging-plus-cfDNA model outperformed either component alone, with an AUC of 0.950 (95% CI 0.926–0.975) in the internal test set and 0.966 (0.940–0.991) on external validation. A companion invasion-prediction model stratified aggressiveness, separating adenocarcinoma in situ from minimally invasive and invasive adenocarcinoma.
impact: The indeterminate nodule is the commonest unresolved problem in thoracic surgery, and the two available signals — how it looks and what is circulating — have been read separately. Combining structural imaging with molecular fragmentation is where the complementary information is, particularly for small or radiologically ambiguous lesions.
practical: This is a model development and validation study. An AUC of 0.95 on a curated test set is not the same as prospective performance in a screening clinic, where prevalence is lower and the model will be applied to nodules unlike those it was trained on. Nothing here is in any guideline, and no assay is available to order. The right use of it is to know the direction the field is moving and to read the eventual prospective work critically — specifically, whether the model beats a validated clinical risk calculator in the same patients, which is the comparison that decides whether it changes anything.
link: Risk-stratified classification of pulmonary nodule malignancy via a machine learning model integrating imaging and cell-free DNA (DECIPHER-NODL)

verify.status: matched with corrections — model real and strong, but it is not prospective and not in any guideline
verify.note: The study is real and better than its odd name suggests — Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2025, deep-learning LDCT radiomics plus a four-feature cfDNA fragmentomics model, stacked ensemble, AUC 0.950 internal and 0.966 external validation, with an additional invasion-prediction model. This is the fifth time in this review that a claim reading as fabricated has turned out to be real; the failure mode remains overstated sourcing, not invented science. Three corrections. (1) The submission calls it a 'prospective AI framework' validated 'across 1,350+ indeterminate pulmonary nodules'; the publication is a model DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION study, and the 1,350 figure could not be verified. (2) 'diagnostic accuracy superior to traditional Brock and Mayo clinical risk models' could not be verified from accessible sources — the documented comparison is against the individual imaging and cfDNA models, not against Brock or Mayo — so that claim has been reframed as the comparison the field still needs. (3) The submission says it 'integrates multi-modal AI nodule risk stratification INTO CLINICAL GUIDELINES'; it is in none, and no assay is orderable. Removed the claim that it 'significantly reduces unnecessary diagnostic resections', which is an aspiration of the framework rather than a measured outcome.

title: RAMIE and Left Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Nodal Yield
breakthrough: Meta-analyses of robot-assisted minimally invasive esophagectomy against conventional minimally invasive esophagectomy consistently find a higher nodal yield, with the advantage concentrated in the left recurrent laryngeal nerve station. Reported effects: left RLN nodes 1.74 versus 1.34 (mean difference 0.22, P<0.001) in one synthesis; a mean difference of 0.60 (95% CI 0.13–1.08, P=0.01) for left RLN nodes and 2.01 (1.05–2.96, P<0.001) for total nodes in another. The technical explanation is the exposure the robot gives in the upper mediastinum, where the left RLN dissection is the hardest part of a two-field lymphadenectomy to do well thoracoscopically.
impact: Left RLN nodal dissection is both the highest-yield and the highest-risk part of the operation — it is where nodal staging is won and where vocal cord palsy is caused. A platform that improves access to that station addresses the specific technical bottleneck.
practical: Look at the effect sizes before quoting this. A difference of 0.22 to 0.60 nodes at the left RLN station is statistically robust across meta-analyses and clinically small — it is a fraction of one node per patient, not a transformed lymphadenectomy. It may still matter, because a single positive station changes stage, but 'significantly higher' should not be heard as 'substantially higher'. What is worth taking seriously is the mechanism: whatever platform is used, the left RLN station needs deliberate, unhurried dissection with nerve preservation as an explicit goal, and intraoperative nerve monitoring is a reasonable adjunct. Vocal cord function should be assessed after the operation, not assumed.
link: Short-term outcomes of robot-assisted versus conventional minimally invasive esophagectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis

verify.status: matched with corrections — direction confirmed, magnitude and guideline status overstated
verify.note: The finding is real and reproducible across several meta-analyses: RAMIE yields more total nodes and more left recurrent laryngeal nerve nodes than conventional minimally invasive esophagectomy, and the left RLN station is where the technical advantage lies. Corrections. (1) MAGNITUDE: the submission says RAMIE 'yields SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER lymph node harvest in the left RLN station', which is true statistically and misleading practically — the published differences are 1.74 versus 1.34 nodes (MD 0.22) and MD 0.60. Stated numerically so the reader can judge. (2) The submission claims this 'establishes RAMIE as a PRIMARY RECOMMENDED SURGICAL MODALITY in ISDE and ESMO practice guidelines for locally advanced esophageal carcinoma'. Neither guideline could be verified as making that recommendation; removed. (3) The submission asserts RAMIE 'mitigat[es] postoperative vocal cord paralysis' — the fewer pulmonary complications finding is supported, but a reduction in RLN palsy specifically could not be verified and would be counterintuitive given that the advantage is MORE aggressive dissection at that nerve. Replaced with the practical instruction (deliberate dissection, consider nerve monitoring, assess cord function postoperatively) rather than a reassurance.
